content: Tinidazole is a medication that has been associated with potential risks. A similar drug has been shown to cause cancer in laboratory animals. It is important to discuss the risks and benefits of using this medication with your doctor. Tinidazole is prescribed to treat specific infections, including trichomoniasis (a sexually transmitted infection affecting both men and women), giardiasis (an intestinal infection causing diarrhea, gas, and stomach cramps), and amebiasis (an intestinal infection that can cause diarrhea, gas, stomach cramps, and may spread to other organs like the liver). Tinidazole belongs to a class of drugs called antiprotozoal agents and works by killing the organisms responsible for these infections. Tinidazole is available as a liquid suspension prepared by a pharmacist or as a tablet, both taken orally. It is typically taken with food, either as a single dose or once daily for 3 to 5 days. If prescribed for multiple days, take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not take more or less of the medication or take it more frequently than prescribed. Shake the liquid form well before each use to ensure even mixing. Complete the full course of the medication, even if you feel better, as stopping too soon or skipping doses may result in incomplete treatment of the infection and antibiotic resistance. Tinidazole may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Before taking tinidazole, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to tinidazole, metronidazole (Flagyl), or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. This includes medications such as erythromycin, ethosuximide, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, HIV protease inhibitors (e.g., indinavir, ritonavir), isoniazid, lithium, metronidazole, nefazodone, oral contraceptives, phenytoin, rifampin, tacrolimus, and others. If you are taking disulfiram (Antabuse) or have stopped taking it within the past two weeks, inform your doctor. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you for side effects. If you are taking cholestyramine (Questran), do not take it at the same time as tinidazole. Ask your doctor or pharmacist how to space the doses of these medications. Inform your doctor if you currently have a yeast infection, are undergoing dialysis, or have a history of seizures, nervous system disorders, blood disorders, or liver disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or become pregnant while taking tinidazole, notify your doctor immediately. Do not breastfeed while taking tinidazole and for three days after completing treatment. Avoid alcohol while taking tinidazole and for three days afterward, as it may cause stomach upset, vomiting, cramps, headaches, sweating, and facial flushing. Discuss with your doctor whether you can consume grapefruit juice while taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Tinidazole may cause side effects. Minor side effects include a sharp, unpleasant metallic taste, upset stomach, vomiting, loss of appetite, constipation, stomach pain or cramps, headache, tiredness or weakness, and dizziness. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects are rare but require immediate medical attention. These include seizures, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, rash, hives, swelling of the face, throat, tongue, lips, eyes, hands, feet, ankles, or lower legs, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing or breathing. If you experience any of these, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store tinidazole in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Discard any unused liquid after seven days. Consult your pharmacist about proper disposal of unused medication. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor may order tests to monitor your response to tinidazole. Inform your doctor and laboratory personnel that you are taking tinidazole before undergoing any tests. Do not share your medication with others. Your prescription is likely not refillable. If your symptoms persist after completing the medication, contact your doctor.
